newsitem.title: UK: N.Ireland's three-year-old peace process in gloom.
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland's three-year-old peace process in gloom.

text.p: Prospects for an end to violence look bleak in Northern Ireland three years after London and Dublin launched a peace process intended to end a quarter of a century of sectarian strife.

The Irish Republican Army (IRA) has ruled out its traditional Christmas truce and Britain and Ireland are at odds over when to let the guerrillas' political wing, Sinn Fein, into the peace talks launched by the "Downing Street Declaration" made on December 15, 1993.
On Thursday, police discovered an IRA mortar bomb they said was intended to kill security forces as they evacuated the area around an army barracks following a hoaxed bomb warning.
And in Ballymena, northwest of Belfast, homes have been firebombed and Catholics have been beaten and harangued by Protestants for the past three months as they go to Mass.

"On the positive side, a lot of people are here who would have been dead (if not for the Downing Street Declaration) but I would say the outcome has been mostly negative," said Richard English of the University of Ulster.
Protestant guerrillas are still honouring a two-year-old ceasefire which has enabled their political allies to take part in the peace talks.
But the IRA abandoned its truce after 17 months, accusing Britain of putting up obstacles to Sinn Fein joining the forum.

The republican guerrillas launched a series of attacks in mainland Britain and scored a huge coup in October by planting two car bombs inside Britain's main army base in Northern Ireland. That attack killed a soldier and wounded 30 people.
Now after a period of quiet, the province is braced for a new onslaught from the IRA after British Prime Minister John Major effectively ruled out any new concessions to Sinn Fein.
Sinn Fein said on Thursday the British army had detained the republican party's president, Gerry Adams, and a party colleague. But security sources denied the pair had been held.
A cache of mortars was discovered last week at a house in west Belfast and Irish police have reported the highest level of IRA activity along their border since the 1994 ceasefires.

A few days ago, Britain's minister for Northern Ireland, Sir Patrick Mayhew, said the peace dividend from the truces had been reversed and he announced a 120 million-pound ($198 million) increase in security spending for the next three years.
The funds were needed not only because of the threat of new IRA attacks, but because of a heightening of sectarian conflict which resulted in some of the worst violence for many years.
There were riots and clashes across the province in the summer after police banned or diverted marches by Protestant "Orange Lodge" members, which Catholics see as provocative.
In one night during riots at Drumcree south of Belfast, 900 petrol bombs were thrown.
English believes the peace process itself is to blame for the rise in tension. "It is really based on a misunderstanding of what is possible," he said.
"The nationalists' hopes that their demands will be met have been raised unreasonably, while the Protestants are afraid that too much has been conceded to the nationalists," he said.
Protestants fear the peace process will end up favouring the Catholics and that they will end up under Dublin's rule.
But Sinn Fein has not yet even gained entry to the talks.

Republicans accuse Major of bowing to pressure from Protestant unionist politicians in refusing to agree to Irish Prime Minister John Bruton's wish that Sinn Fein be allowed to join the talks soon after the IRA calls a new truce.
Major's Conservatives have lost their majority in parliament and he depends heavily for support on the unionists in parliament.
